rewriteLast.title: Chapter 5 · A Simpler Way
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a family of five and a young woman in a plain dress packing a grand parlor into wooden crates, silk gowns folded into a trunk, a small girl carrying her doll on top of a pile, shafts of winter light through tall windows, gentle storybook illustration

blocks.text: The great Shaw house came down around its family like a tent being folded. Servants said goodbye at the door, one by one. The fine carriages were sold. The silk gowns were packed away in trunks. Crates stood in the marble hall where the piano used to be. Mr. Shaw, who had sat with his head in his hands since the bank failed, looked up one morning. “We shall move to a small house,” he said, “and live plainly, like an honest family.” The move was to be made before the month was out. There was a strange lift in the house, like a held breath let go.
The marble hall fills with crates, and the family folds its tent.

The move was hard in ways nobody had guessed. Fanny did not know how to make a bed, and was ashamed to learn. Tom, who had come home from his office to help, carried trunks till his hands were sore. He said nothing, which was his way of saying much. Maud, the little one, grieved for her dolls’ grand house. She was learning, at six, that dolls can live happily in a shoe box.
Talk together: the Shaws lost their riches in one morning. What could they still count on that no bank could take?

Polly came every day with her sleeves rolled up. She showed Fanny how to fold and Maud how to dust. She made jokes over the crates till the packing went like a game. On the first evening in the small house they ate plain suppers off a deal table. And Mr. Shaw said it tasted better than any dinner the marble hall ever saw. Though nobody quite believed him yet, everybody hoped he was right. And hoping together was new, and not unpleasant. Maud made a house for her dolls under the deal table. It became the best-loved room in the small house.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · Fanny's Beaus
chapters.artPrompt: a pretty young woman in a faded silk dress standing at a window with lace curtains drawn back, watching elegant carriages pass in the street below without stopping, her face proud and lonely, a young woman in a plain dress standing kindly at her shoulder, gray winter light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: When the Shaws were rich, Fanny’s parlor was never quiet. Young men came with flowers and compliments, and Fanny danced through the season like the belle of the ball. When the money failed, the carriages stopped at the door. The compliments went with them. Fanny stood at the window and watched elegant parties pass to other houses. She had believed, till now, that she was the kind of person people came to see. She learned in one winter what no lecture ever taught her. And the lesson had thorns in it.
The carriages roll past the door, and Fanny counts who does not come.

“They liked my father’s money, not me,” she said one gray afternoon, with a hard little laugh. “I have been courted like a bank.” Polly did not say I told you so. She sat down and said the only thing worth saying. “Then now you will find out who likes Fanny.” And to Fanny’s great surprise, one or two true friends did come. They came quietly, with books and work-baskets instead of flowers.
Talk together: Fanny’s crowd was large when she was rich and small when she was poor. Which crowd would you rather have, and why?

It stung, and then it healed into something stronger. Fanny began to see that she had spent her seasons collecting admirers the way other people collect stamps. None of them could be spent on a rainy day. She took to visiting Polly’s little room. And she found that poverty, shared with a friend, was lighter than riches shared with flatterers. That was a curious bargain, but it was a true one. Fanny learned to darn, and to laugh at her own thimbled thumbs. She liked the quiet afternoons better than the crowded ones. One of the true friends was a poor governess Fanny had once snubbed at a party. Fanny went to her first, and the going was the hardest step she ever took. It led to the easiest friendship of her life.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · The Dressing Room
chapters.artPrompt: a grand dressing room with girls in silk petticoats being laced tight before tall mirrors, one girl in a simple loose dress standing apart holding her own plain gown, gaslight and perfume bottles, a fainting girl on a chaise behind, warm but uneasy light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: One afternoon Fanny took Polly to a grand friend’s house before a party, and Polly walked into a battlefield. The dressing room was full of girls being pinched and painted into fashion. One had already fainted on the chaise. She was being revived with salts so she could be laced some more. Polly stood in her simple dress and felt as if she had strayed into a strange, sad country. And the smell of rouge and held breath was in the air.
The laces pull and the mirrors sparkle, and Polly wonders at the price of fashion.

“Why do you do it?” she asked plainly. The girls laughed at first — country manners, they said. But Polly only opened her cloak to show a strong, healthy frame that ran, walked, and breathed freely. “I have never fainted in my life,” she said. “I should like to see one of you try a month of my way. Loose clothes, open windows, and a good run before breakfast.” The girls laughed again. But one of them wrote the words down in her fan.
Question for you: the fashion of that day hurt healthy girls. What fashions today might cost more than they look?

A seed was planted. Before the season was out, two of the girls had taken to morning walks. One had quietly loosened her laces, and owned in secret that she felt like a new creature. Polly went home in her plain gown, glad of her strong young body and her free breath. And half the dressing room envied her more than the richest bride there. Not one of them said so aloud. The friend’s name was Belle, and her dressing room smelled of violet powder and defiance. Polly counted four mirrors, nine hairpins on the floor, and one open window, which was shut at once. She opened it again gently, and no one dared to stop her.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · Maud and Polly
chapters.artPrompt: a small girl in a pinafore sitting on the floor of a modest parlor teaching her doll to sew on a scrap of cloth, a young woman in a plain dress kneeling beside her with a needle and thread, a small stove and a cat, warm afternoon light, sweet storybook illustration

blocks.text: Of all the Shaw family, little Maud changed the most. She had been a spoilt little pouter, scolding and demanding like a very small empress. But trouble had tumbled her empire flat. In the ruins she discovered Polly. Polly never gave her everything she wanted. Polly taught her to sew doll clothes, to do her share of the dusting, and to say she was sorry. Maud had once believed the last of these quite impossible.
A doll, a needle, and a small empress learning the sweeter trade of being a child.

Maud adored her for it. Children always adore the people who make them grow. She would sit at Polly’s knee by the hour, sewing crooked stitches on her doll’s new gown. And she heard about the country, the farm, and a mother far away who was wise and good. “When I am big,” Maud announced, “I shall be like Polly.” And the whole family, hearing it, decided there were worse ambitions in the world.
Talk together: Maud gave up being an empress to become a child. What is the difference between being waited on and being loved?

The funny part was that Maud grew prettier as she grew sweeter. The pouting face smoothed out into smiles. The small tyrant’s voice turned into a pleasant one. Grandma said it first, over her knitting. “Polly has done more for that child in six months than fine schools and finer dresses did in six years.” And nobody in the small house disagreed. Least of all Maud, who was busy teaching her doll to say sorry too. Polly never took the credit. She only said that Maud had been sweet all along, under the empress. Maud’s doll was named Elfrida, and had once owned a carriage and six dresses. Elfrida learned to say sorry first, and Maud followed a week later. The family agreed it was the best education in the house.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · Tom at Work
chapters.artPrompt: a young man of about twenty in a plain dark suit walking briskly to a brick office building at sunrise, a roll of papers under his arm, his head high, shop shutters opening along the street, pale gold morning light, hopeful storybook illustration

blocks.text: Tom Shaw, who had been the scamp of the family, turned out to have a spine in him after all. He went to work at a merchant’s office. He walked to save carfare, and learned his sums like a man paying his own way. His father, who had scolded Tom for years, now watched him in silence. He was prouder than he could say, and he never said it, which Tom understood perfectly.
Tom walks to the office in the gray dawn, and carries his own weight at last.

He still fell into scrapes, for that was Tom’s nature. An ink bottle perished, a ledger went astray. But he owned them like a man and paid for them out of his small salary. On Sundays he tramped across town to the little house. Ostensibly he came to see his people; really he came to see Polly. She helped him with his accounts and his temper, and both improved. His father noticed the Sundays too, and smiled into his paper.
New word: salary — the money a worker earns for his work. Tom’s was small, but every coin of it was honestly his.

“I am not a genius,” Tom told Polly honestly, one Sunday by her small stove. “I shall never be a brilliant fellow. But I mean to be a good one, if you will keep on telling me the truth.” Polly laughed and promised to keep on. And privately she thought this: a good, true man beats a brilliant one any day of the week. Especially a rainy Sunday one. Sunday by Sunday, the little stove seemed to hold more summers than the marble hall ever had. The office taught Tom what school never could: that minutes are money and words are promises. He kept a little ledger of his own now, and ruled the lines straight. The ledger had one column marked P, and Tom did not explain it to anyone.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · Polly's Little Room
chapters.artPrompt: a modest top-floor room with a small iron stove, an upright piano against the wall covered with a warm cloth, sheet music on a table, a girl mending a glove by the window with snow falling outside, a kettle on the stove, quiet winter light, gentle storybook illustration

blocks.text: Polly’s own life was not easy, whatever her face said. Her lodging was one room at the top of a tall house, cold till the stove caught. The wind played tunes round the window. Her music pupils came slow and paid slower. Rent was due like the day, every seven days, whether the piano earned it or not. Polly darned her gloves, turned her coats, and sang while she worked. And her songs were mostly cheerful, which told the truth.
A kettle, a stove, and one brave girl keeping a small light in a tall cold house.

She sent money home to the village, for there were younger ones to help through school. She never once spoke of doing it. Fanny found out by accident and could not sleep for shame of her own old complaints. The next day Fanny appeared with a basket: real coffee, coal, and a warm shawl. The two girls cried and laughed over it together. The shawl was worn for years, and loved the most of any in the house.
Talk together: Polly never begged and never boasted. Why is quiet pride sometimes harder than asking for help?

“I earn my bread,” Polly wrote to her mother, “and it is sweet bread, though it is plain.” She kept one luxury she would not give up: Sunday evenings. Then the Shaw family crowded into her little room for songs round the stove. The room held eight people and one small stove. It held all the warmth in the city, so far as anybody could tell. And the tall cold house, for one evening a week, was the warmest place in town. Polly taught Maud her first song that winter. Maud practiced it till the whole house could sing it asleep. The wind kept her awake some nights, and Polly made up songs to the rhythm of it. Her mother would have said the songs were worth more than the rent, and Polly believed her.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · Summer in the Village
chapters.artPrompt: a young woman in a light summer dress walking a country lane with a basket of wildflowers, an old farmhouse with hollyhocks ahead, grazing cows in green meadows beyond, her face resting and glad, bright summer noon, warm storybook illustration

blocks.text: When the teaching year ended, Polly packed her little trunk and went home to the village for the summer. The stagecoach set her down by the old signpost. The walk up the lane smelled of hay and clover. Her mother stood at the farmhouse gate in a clean apron. Polly, who had not cried all winter, cried now, comfortably, into a shoulder that smelled of bread and lavender. And the gate stayed open all summer, which is what gates are for.
The lane, the hollyhocks, and a mother waiting at the gate.

That summer was a medicine no city doctor could have mixed. Polly slept under a quilt with the window open. She taught the village children their singing on Sundays. She picked berries, and read aloud to her mother in the evenings. The letters she got from the small Shaw house were read so often they grew soft at the folds. She read them out loud too, so that her mother knew them by heart.
Talk together: Polly went home to rest, not to hide. What is the difference between resting and giving up?

“You are thinner, and you are better,” her mother said at the summer’s end. “The city is using you, Polly, but it is not spoiling you. Remember that money and fashion are weather. Truth and love are climate.” Polly carried that saying back to town like a smooth stone in her pocket. As a girl she had carried her mother’s other words the same way, and they had never yet worn out. On the last evening she picked a bunch of her mother’s lavender to take back with her. It went in the music roll. There was time in the village for everything the city had crowded out. There was whittling, wading, watching clouds, and doing nothing at all on purpose. Polly came back brown and slow-spoken. The city looked different from her window now, larger and less loud.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · Back to the City
chapters.artPrompt: a young woman with a small trunk and a music roll stepping down from a hansom cab before a modest brick house, a small girl in a pinafore running down the steps to meet her, autumn leaves blowing along the pavement, soft golden morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Autumn found Polly back in the city, with two more pupils won by her summer’s rest. She had a plan written in her neat hand: earn, save, help, and keep cheerful. Maud saw her from the window of the small Shaw house and ran down the street with her pinafore flying. The little house felt incomplete, Polly said, until her music roll stood in its corner again. And then it felt complete, which settled the matter.
Maud runs to meet the coach, and the little house feels whole again.

The winter filled up with work. There were lessons morning and evening, and a singing class on Thursdays. There were clothes to make over for the whole small household. Fanny now sewed like a comrade instead of a fine lady. Tom built Polly a little bookshelf for her room. He hammered it in the shed and swore at his thumbs. It was crooked. It was the finest shelf in the city.
Question for you: Polly plans her year on one sheet of paper. If you planned yours — earn, learn, help, keep cheerful — what would go first?

By Christmas the little circle was warmer than the grand one had ever been. Even Mr. Shaw came on Sunday evenings now. He sat in the corner reading while the young people sang, with his eyes half shut. He looked like a man who had lost a fortune and found his family. And he was not sure, on the whole, that he had lost. The crooked shelf held the singing books, and nobody ever straightened it. The singing class met on Thursdays in the Shaws’ little parlor, and began with three pupils and ended with eleven. Word traveled in that city, when the thing was good. Polly’s plan grew a new line that winter: teach more, worry less. She wrote it in and meant it. Tom’s shelf held her songbooks, and gave her courage every time it creaked.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 · The Grand Party
chapters.artPrompt: a grand ballroom with chandeliers and mirrored walls, a young woman in a simple white muslin gown dancing with natural grace at the center of admiring guests, fashionable girls in silk watching from the edge, a young man watching with quiet pride, warm candlelight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: That winter Fanny was bidden to the grandest party of the season, and she begged Polly to come. Polly had one party dress in the world: a soft white muslin, old-fashioned, clean, and plain. In it she went, with her smooth hair and her straight back. Some silk gowns rustled when she entered. Someone whispered behind a fan that the country cousin had come. And the whisper was meant to wound.
The silk gowns rustle, but the plain white muslin is the one the room remembers.

Then the music began, and the whispering stopped. Polly danced as she did everything: naturally, gladly, with no pins sticking into her. There were no laces pinching her breath away. Her face was happy. And happy faces are the best dress ever invented. By midnight the plain muslin was the center of the brightest circle in the room. Two silk gowns had asked to be introduced. And the fan that had whispered was folded away and still.
Talk together: Polly’s dress cost almost nothing and outshone the silk. What exactly was she wearing, then, that made her shine?

Tom, watching from the doorway, said nothing at all. But he stood straighter for a week afterward. “You were the finest lady there,” Fanny told Polly on the way home, “and you never once tried to be.” Polly laughed in the cold air. “The secret is not trying,” she said. “A girl who is content with herself has both hands free for dancing.” And she had, and it showed. For a week afterward, two or three girls took to smooth hair and straight backs. They found they could breathe and dance better. The supper after the dancing was the gayest part, because Polly could eat without laces strangling her. She and Fanny rode home with their shoes in their laps and their hair down. It was the happiest party either of them remembered, and it was not really about the party at all.
